title: Numbers
subtitle: In the wilderness
lead: Numbers is called in Hebrew Bemidbar, "In the wilderness," from its first verse: "The LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai." Its English name comes from the Greek Arithmoi, "Numbers," after the two great counts of Israel's fighting men in chapters 1 and 26. Between them lies the story of a whole generation. The people who left Egypt are counted, organized and sent out toward the land, and almost all of them die on the way. Their children are counted again on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.

The book moves in three stages. Chapters 1–10 are set at Sinai: the census, the camp around the tent of meeting, the duties of the Levites, laws on the suspected wife and the Nazirite, the priestly blessing, the leaders' gifts and the Passover, until the cloud lifts and the march begins. Chapters 11–21 are the journey: complaints about food, Miriam and Aaron against Moses, the scouts and the people's refusal to enter Canaan, forty years of wandering, Korah's revolt, the water from the rock and the bronze snake. Chapters 22–36 are set on the plains of Moab: Balaam's blessings, the sin at Peor, the second census, Zelophehad's daughters, the calendar of offerings, vows, the war with Midian, and the land's borders and cities.

Numbers mixes lists, laws, stories and poems more freely than any other book of the Torah. Its large figures, its sharp judgments and its strange rites, such as the bitter water of chapter 5 and the red heifer of chapter 19, have puzzled readers for centuries. This site sets out the main ways they are read: as history, by critical scholars, in Jewish tradition and by Christians.
facts: Not named. Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses. Most critical scholars: priestly and non-priestly sources, finished during or after the exile.
Set in the 40 years between Sinai and the Jordan. Critical: written from the monarchy to after the exile.

audience.to: The book presents itself as the LORD's words through Moses to two generations of Israelites. The first are the people who left Egypt, counted at Sinai and then dying in the wilderness of Paran and Zin over forty years. The second are their children, counted again on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, about to enter Canaan. Within that story many laws have their own hearers. Some are for Aaron and his sons, some for the Levite clans, the tribal leaders, husbands and wives, or the heads of the tribes. On most critical views, its first readers were Israelites of the late monarchy or, more often, Judeans of the exile and the Persian period. They had lost the land and were rebuilding a community around the Temple.
audience.why: To show a people on the way what it means to live with God at the center and what happens when they will not trust him. Chapters 1–10 set Israel in order around the tent. Chapters 11–25 tell how that generation complained, refused the land and died, though even Balaam could not curse them. Chapters 26–36 count the new generation and give it laws for the land. These cover inheritance, offerings, vows, borders and refuge. Knowing the audience changes the reading. For readers who had lost the land, the death of the old generation was a warning. The laws for the children were a promise that God's plan had not ended.
views: Moses for the generation in the wilderness

Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses wrote the book for the Israelites of the wilderness and their children. The book itself says only that Moses wrote down the stages of the journey (33:2). Conservative scholars such as Wenham and Ashley point to its camp and travel details and its desert setting.
Sources from the monarchy and after
Wellhausen, Noth and Baden: older non-priestly stories, written under the kings, were joined to priestly laws and lists. The finished book spoke to Judeans during or after the exile.
Priestly law of the First Temple

Kaufmann, Haran and Milgrom: the priestly laws and lists of Numbers were written before the exile, for the priests and worshipers of the First Temple. Milgrom points to old terms and to the tithe given to the Levites (18:21).

Many European scholars: Numbers was among the last books of the Torah to be finished. It was written after the exile to join the priestly laws to Deuteronomy. It answered the Second Temple community's questions about priests, Levites and land.

Olson: whatever its sources, the finished book is built on its two censuses, the death of the old generation and the birth of the new. Every later reader is invited to stand with the second generation at the edge of the land.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading: Israel's forty years in the wilderness happened as recorded, with a census of about 600,000 fighting men. Some who hold the book historical read the Hebrew 'elef in the census as 'clan' or 'unit' rather than 'thousand', giving a much smaller number (Mendenhall, Humphreys).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars read Numbers as a late weaving of priestly and older traditions, with idealized numbers and itineraries shaped by later geography and the needs of Israel after the exile.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis call it Bemidbar, 'In the Wilderness'. The Sifre, the Talmud, Rashi and Ramban read its rebellions as lessons for every generation, and its priestly blessing (6:24–26) is still spoken in synagogues.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The New Testament reads the wilderness as a warning and a pattern: the bronze serpent lifted up (John 3:14), the rock that was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), the generation that fell short of rest (Hebrews 3–4), and Balaam's star (Matthew 2).

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. It is built line by line from the Hebrew words in their own order rather than adapted from another English version. YHWH is "the LORD." Key words are kept steady across the Torah: korban is "offering," olah "burnt offering," hatta't "sin offering" (some scholars prefer "purification offering"), 'edah "community," ohel mo'ed "tent of meeting," mishkan "tabernacle," kapporet "atonement lid," hesed "loyal love" and tsara'at "skin disease," never "leprosy." The census verb paqad is "enroll" and pequdim "those enrolled"; nasi' is "leader"; the Levites' mishmeret is "duty" or "guard"; tekhelet is "blue-violet." As in Leviticus, a worshiper "leans" his hand on an offering (samakh), the handful burned from a grain offering is its "token portion" (azkarah), ma'al is to "act unfaithfully," and hiqriv is "present." These renderings are shared with the rest of the site. The census figures are given as the Hebrew has them; the notes explain other ways to read 'elef, "thousand." The poems, such as the priestly blessing (6:24–26), the ark songs (10:35–36) and Balaam's oracles (chapters 23–24), are set as verse.

Where the Masoretic Text differs from the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint or the Dead Sea Scrolls in a way that matters, the variant is shown beside the verse. Examples are the Samaritan additions from Deuteronomy (10:10, and in chapters 12–14, 20, 21, 27 and 31), the Septuagint's order of 10:34–36, and the readings of the Qumran scroll 4QNum-b.

KJV, ASV, WEB, YLT

Public-domain English versions. The KJV (1611, standard text of 1769) prints words the translators added in italics. Young's Literal Translation (1898) keeps Hebrew word order and tenses.

BSB

The Berean Standard Bible, a modern translation released into the public domain.

Hebrew

The Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), as edited by the Westminster Leningrad Codex project and corrected in STEPBible's TAHOT (Tyndale House, Cambridge), with each word's meaning and grammar.

Numbers can seem like a jumble: a census, then a list of camp positions, then a law about jealous husbands, then a long list of gifts repeated twelve times. Three keys help. First, follow the places. The book moves from Sinai (1:1–10:10) through the wilderness to Kadesh (10:11–21:35) and on to the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13). Second, follow the generations. The first census counts the people who left Egypt; by the second, "not one man" of them is left except Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65). Third, notice how law and story take turns. Laws about holiness and the camp come right before the stories where holiness is broken, and the laws of chapters 15 and 27–36 look ahead to life in the land, even after the first generation's failure.

Chapters 1–10 show Israel as it should be: every tribe counted, every Levite clan given its job, the tent at the center, the cloud above, the trumpets ready. From chapter 11 on, the same people complain, rebel and die. The contrast is the book's main lesson for both Jews and Christians: being organized around God is not the same as trusting him.

The first census gives 603,550 men of fighting age (1:46), and the second 601,730 (26:51). With women, children and Levites that suggests two million people or more in the Sinai desert. Readers answer this in four main ways. Many traditional readers take the figures at face value and point to God's care in the desert. Others, following Flinders Petrie, George Mendenhall and Colin Humphreys, read 'elef as a clan or military unit, giving a few thousand fighting men. Some look for symbolic meaning or number patterns. Most critical scholars treat the lists as idealized, perhaps based on a later census. The notes on 1:46 and the chapter 1 page set out each view and its problems, such as the small number of firstborn in 3:43.

In the synagogue Numbers is read from early summer, in ten weekly portions, and the first, Bemidbar, usually falls just before the Feast of Weeks. The main rabbinic commentary is the Sifre on Numbers, a legal midrash on chapters 5–35, with the later Numbers Rabbah. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban read the book closely for its law and its lessons. Several passages are part of Jewish life today: the priestly blessing (6:24–26), said by the kohanim in the synagogue and by parents over their children on Friday night; the tassels of 15:37–41, recited daily in the Shema; the words "How good are your tents, Jacob" (24:5), said on entering a synagogue; the second Passover (9:9–14); and the release of vows (chapter 30). The rabbis read the complaints and rebellions as warnings, and the Mishnah counts ten times that Israel tested God in the wilderness (Mishnah Avot 5:4).

Paul tells the Corinthians that the wilderness stories "happened to them as examples" and lists the craving, the idolatry, the testing and the grumbling of Numbers (1 Corinthians 10:1–11). Hebrews 3–4 reads the refusal at Kadesh as the classic failure of faith that keeps people from God's rest. Jesus compares his being lifted up to the bronze snake (John 3:14–15). Balaam appears in 2 Peter 2:15, Jude 11 and Revelation 2:14 as the model of a teacher who sells his gift, and his "star out of Jacob" (24:17) was read by many church fathers as a prophecy of Christ, linked with the star of Matthew 2. Origen's homilies on Numbers read the camp, the march and the stages of chapter 33 as the soul's journey toward God. Many churches use the priestly blessing at the end of worship.

The Masoretic Text of Numbers is generally well kept. The Samaritan Pentateuch has a longer form that copies Moses' speeches from Deuteronomy 1–3 into Numbers, at 10:10 and in chapters 12–14, 20, 21, 27 and 31, so that the two books agree. A Dead Sea Scroll, 4QNum-b, from about the turn of the era, preserves parts of chapters 11–36 and often shares these longer readings, which shows that this form was in use before the Samaritans' later text. The Septuagint differs in some numbers, adds small phrases, and places 10:34 after the ark songs of 10:35–36. In Hebrew manuscripts those two verses are set off by inverted nun marks, and the rabbis called them a book of their own. Numbers also has several of the Bible's dotted words (3:39; 9:10; 21:30; 29:15), which scribes marked as doubtful.

spec.title: Numbers as the book of the march
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Numbers is organized by the verb nasa', "set out, pull up stakes." Chapters 1–10 build a people that can move: a counted army, a camp arranged around the tent, Levites trained to take it down, trumpets to signal, and the cloud to give the order "at the LORD's word" (9:18). The first real march begins at 10:11. Then the stories ask whether the people will actually go, and at Kadesh they refuse (14:1–4). The rest of the book is the slow march of the next generation, listed stage by stage in chapter 33, until it stands at the Jordan. Read this way, the long lists are not filler. They are the preparation for a journey, and the failures are a journey refused. Parts of this reading overlap with Dennis Olson's two-generation outline, with Jacob Milgrom's attention to the camp, and with Rolf Knierim and George Coats, who read the book's genre as the story of a campaign on the march (FOTL, 2005); the focus on the verb is my own suggestion.

authorship: The book repeats that "the LORD spoke to Moses," and 33:2 says that "Moses wrote down their starting points" on the journey. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a) and the church fathers took Moses as the author of the whole Torah. Conservative scholars such as Gordon Wenham and Timothy Ashley point to the book's desert setting, to its camp and travel details, and to Egyptian and Near Eastern parallels, while allowing for later notes such as 12:3 on Moses' humility.

Since Julius Wellhausen most critical scholars have divided Numbers between the Priestly source (P), which holds chapters 1–10, most laws and the lists, and older non-priestly stories (J and E) in parts of chapters 10–14, 16, 20–25 and 32. Martin Noth thought the book had no plan of its own and was mostly late additions. Joel Baden and others still defend a source analysis.
Later editors and a late book

Many European scholars now see Numbers as one of the last books of the Torah to be finished, a bridge written after the exile to link the priestly material of Exodus and Leviticus with Deuteronomy. On this view its laws answer questions of the Second Temple period.

Dennis Olson argued that, however it was written, the finished book has a clear plan built on its two censuses: the death of the old generation (1–25) and the birth of the new (26–36). Many readers of all views now follow this outline.
